articles.title: Rochdale Council to Implement New Planning Decision Guidelines from October 31
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Council is set to adopt new planning decision guidelines mandated by the Government, which will change how planning applications are processed across the borough starting October 31.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Council is preparing to implement significant changes to the way planning applications are decided, following new Government guidance. These changes will take effect on October 31, 2026, as mandated by the Town and Country Planning (Discharge of Local Planning Authority Functions) (England) Regulations 2026.

The new regulations aim to streamline the planning process by allowing planning officers to determine a greater number of applications. This shift is intended to enable planning committees to focus on larger applications and more complex issues. Under the new guidelines, certain applications will be designated for officer determination and will not be presented to the committee unless referred by a nominated councillor and a council officer.

Additionally, ward councillors will no longer have the ability to automatically call-in applications for committee consideration, nor will there be a threshold for objections that would trigger such a review. This is expected to provide greater clarity and consistency in the decision-making process, according to a report prepared for the council.

On Thursday, Rochdale Council will be asked to formally adopt these changes. Members of the council will still be able to engage with the planning process, raise concerns from residents, and submit material planning reasons, although a member request will not automatically necessitate committee determination.

articles.title: Man Injured in Altercation on Rochdale Road, Middleton
articles.excerpt: A man sustained injuries during an altercation on Rochdale Road in Middleton on October 11, prompting a response from police and ambulances shortly after the incident.
articles.content_html:
A man was injured during an altercation on Rochdale Road in Middleton on the afternoon of October 11. Greater Manchester Police received reports of a disturbance at approximately 4:30pm and dispatched several police cars and two ambulances to the scene.

Upon arrival, officers located the injured man, whose injuries are not believed to be life-threatening. The exact circumstances surrounding the incident remain unclear as investigations are ongoing, according to a police statement.

The police confirmed that they are working to determine the full details of the incident. No further information regarding potential suspects or the nature of the altercation has been released.

Local residents may notice an increased police presence on Rochdale Road as inquiries continue. Anyone with information about the incident is encouraged to contact the authorities.

articles.title: Rochdale Borough Council Approves VCFSE Accord for 2026-2035
articles.excerpt: The Rochdale Borough Council has officially signed off on the VCFSE Accord, outlining plans for the voluntary, community, faith and social enterprise sector from 2026 to 2035.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has approved the VCFSE Accord for the period 2026 to 2035, a strategic framework aimed at enhancing collaboration within the voluntary, community, faith and social enterprise sector.

The decision was made public on 11 October 2026 and is part of the council's ongoing commitment to support local organisations and improve community services.

The Accord outlines key priorities and actions that will guide the development of the sector over the next decade, ensuring that local needs are met effectively.

Next steps will involve the implementation of the Accord, with further details expected to be shared with stakeholders in the coming months.

articles.title: M62 Westbound Closed Between Junctions 22 and 21 After Multi-Vehicle Collision
articles.excerpt: The M62 westbound remains closed between Junction 22 at Denshaw and Junction 21 at Rochdale following a serious multi-vehicle crash that occurred late on Saturday night.
articles.content_html:
The M62 westbound carriageway in Greater Manchester is closed between Junction 22 (Denshaw) and Junction 21 (Rochdale) following a serious multi-vehicle collision that occurred shortly before 11 pm on Saturday, October 10. Emergency services, including Greater Manchester Police and National Highways traffic officers, are currently at the scene managing the incident.

As of 6:30 am on Sunday, October 11, the westbound carriageway remains fully closed. Motorists are advised to check for the latest traffic updates and allow extra time for their journeys if travelling through the affected area. National Highways has confirmed that the closure is necessary due to the serious nature of the crash, although further details regarding the vehicles involved and any potential injuries have not yet been disclosed.

Drivers approaching the closure are urged to follow official instructions and temporary road signs, as traffic arrangements may change while emergency services respond to the incident. It is recommended that motorists avoid entering the closed section and consider alternative routes, checking for congestion on surrounding roads before making a decision.

For those travelling westbound towards Rochdale, it is important to follow the diversion routes issued by National Highways. The appropriate diversion may vary depending on the driver's location and destination. Updates from Greater Manchester Police and National Highways will provide verified information as the situation develops.

articles.title: Why Rochdale says “cruckle”
articles.excerpt: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.summary: How a tiny local verb — to “cruckle” — links everyday speech in Rochdale to older northern dialects and why linguists care.
articles.body:
Anyone from Rochdale who’s ever limped away from a small mishap will recognise the line: “I cruckled my ankle.” For many locals, cruckle means the particular half‑twist or awkward roll of the foot you can often walk off — not a full sprain but a sudden wobble that makes you wince. This usage is recorded in contemporary perceptual descriptions of Greater Manchester speech and has been listed by residents when describing Rochdale’s spoken character. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

The word itself, however, has deeper roots. Historical dialect lexicography gives us a family of related forms — crookle, crukle, cruggle, krukel — all clustered around meanings such as to bend, make crooked, stoop, huddle or hobble. Late‑19th and early‑20th‑century dialect sources and Scottish dialect records preserve these cognates, showing the same phonetic shape and similar senses across northern English and Scots varieties. In the Dictionary of the Scots Language you can see cognate entries (kruggle / cruggle / cruckle) used with senses like “to crouch or huddle,” and nineteenth‑century dialect glosses list crookle with senses such as “to make crooked; to bend, twist.” ([dsl.ac.uk](https://dsl.ac.uk/entry/snd00075099))

How did a general sense of bending or crookedness come to mean the small ankle‑roll in Rochdale? Linguists point to ordinary, well‑attested word‑formation processes. A crook/crook‑ family root (suggesting bending, hooking or crookedness) plus a frequentative or diminutive ‑le ending can produce verbs that describe small, repeated, or imitative actions — crook → crookle. Comparable northern and Germanic dialect forms show similar semantic shifts from ‘bend’ or ‘stoop’ toward senses connected with awkward gait or limping; the broader comparative work on Germanic dialect vocabularies helps explain why these forms and meanings sit together. In short, cruckle is linguistically predictable as a local survival and narrowing of an older dialect verb family. ([upload.wikimedia.org](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/be/The_semantic_development_of_words_for_%22walk%2C_run%22_in_the_Germanic_languages_%28IA_semanticdevelopm00ihririch%29.pdf))

Is cruckle uniquely Rochdalian? The short answer is: socially, yes — geographically, not absolutely. Perceptual dialect research carried out in Greater Manchester (2024) collected people’s mental maps and comments about local speech; among the keywords used to evoke Rochdale speech were “broad,” “flat,” “guinnel” and “cruckle,” showing that residents and neighbours associate the word particularly with Rochdale. That kind of folk‑linguistic visibility gives a strong local identity to a word even when related forms appear in older records elsewhere. At the same time, historical dictionaries and place‑name evidence show related spellings and senses across northern England and Scotland, so it would be misleading to claim the sound‑type has never occurred outside the area. ([eprints.gla.ac.uk](https://eprints.gla.ac.uk/330652/2/330652.pdf))

Large projects that collect lived speech and crowd‑sourced dialect entries also help explain how such words persist. When the British Library and other public call‑outs gathered regional words, contributors highlighted locally specific items that researchers had not always recorded in older printed dialect dictionaries; popular reportage of that work singled out “cruckle” as an example of a recognisably local term with onomatopoeic appeal. These crowdsourced attestations, together with formal perceptual surveys, are why small words like cruckle keep turning up in contemporary studies of regional identity. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/science/2017/nov/24/british-library-project-discovers-two-new-words-thanks-to-guardian-readers))

What should readers take away? Cruckle matters because it shows how vocabulary anchors place: the word’s form and original sense are old and shared across northern dialects, but memory, everyday use and local attitude have made it feel distinctly Rochdale. Linguists view it as a useful data point — for historical contact between Lancashire and Yorkshire varieties, for small‑scale semantic narrowing, and for how people use language to say where they’re from. If you’ve got family pronunciations, old spellings or written examples from letters, keep them — local archives and dialect projects welcome material that helps trace exactly when and where words like cruckle shifted meaning and stuck to a place.

articles.title: Roadworks Scheduled on Nowell Road, Pershore Road and Thornham Lane in Middleton from 26 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council has announced roadworks that will affect Nowell Road, Pershore Road, and Thornham Lane in Middleton starting on 26 October 2026, with temporary closures expected.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has announced that roadworks will commence on Nowell Road and Pershore Road in Middleton on 26 October 2026. The specific details regarding the duration of the roadworks have not been disclosed, but temporary closures are expected during this period.

In addition to the works on Nowell Road and Pershore Road, Thornham Lane will also undergo roadworks from 26 October 2026. These works will take place daily from 9am to 4pm until 30 October 2026, with part of Thornham Lane closed from the junction with Rochdale Road for 23 metres in an easterly direction.

During the Thornham Lane closure, there will be no alternative route for vehicles, although access will be provided if it is deemed safe to do so. Residents and motorists are advised to plan their journeys accordingly to avoid delays.

For further information, residents can view a map of the roadworks across Greater Manchester on the Rochdale Borough Council website.

articles.title: Construction Completed on Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre in Kingsway Business Park
articles.excerpt: The Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre in Kingsway Business Park has reached a significant construction milestone, marking the completion of the first major development in Atom Valley.
articles.content_html:
Construction work has been completed on the Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre (SMMC) located in Kingsway Business Park, Rochdale. This marks the first major development in the Atom Valley project, which aims to foster economic growth and innovation in the region.

The project commenced last November, with the aim of creating a cutting-edge facility dedicated to materials and manufacturing. On Friday, civic leaders, including Mayor of Rochdale Cllr Faisal Rana, were given a tour of the site and an update on its progress from key figures involved in the project, such as Paul Ormerod, Chair of Atom Valley, and representatives from the University of Manchester and Greater Manchester Combined Authority.

Cllr Rana emphasised the importance of the SMMC, stating that it represents more than just a new building; it signifies investment in the community, job creation, and a commitment to a sustainable future for young people in the area. The centre is part of a broader initiative to position Atom Valley as a leading hub for advanced manufacturing and engineering across Greater Manchester.

With the construction phase now complete, the next steps will involve equipping the centre and preparing for its official opening, which is expected to provide new opportunities for local residents and contribute to the strengthening of the local economy.

Construction of the flagship Sustainable Materials and Manufacturing Centre in Kingsway Business Park is now finished and on Friday, civic leaders were given a tour of the site and an update on progress from Paul Ormerod, Chair of Atom Valley; Cllr Danny Meredith, Cabinet Member for Regeneration and Housing; Prof John Holden of the University of Manchester; Helen Wilding of GMCA; and Dr Liam Britnell, founder of Vector Homes. Mayor of Rochdale Cllr Faisal Rana shared: “This is about so much more than a new building. It is about investment, innovation, creating jobs and building a brighter future for generations to come. “Atom Valley is one of Greater Manchester’s most ambitious growth projects, bringing together Rochdale, Bury and Oldham to create a leading centre for advanced manufacturing, engineering, sustainable materials and new technologies. Building work has now been completed on the SMMC. Image: Paul Waugh “For me, as Mayor, it is particularly encouraging to see projects with the potential to make such a lasting difference to our communities. “Economic growth is not just about investment figures; it is about real opportunities for our residents, good-quality jobs for our young people and a stronger local economy for the future. “Rochdale has a proud industrial heritage, and projects like Atom Valley show how we can build on that legacy while embracing modern technology, sustainable manufacturing and innovation. “Our industrial past helped shape who we are. The Government, the Greater Manchester Combined Authority and Rochdale Borough Council have all invested, working with Rochdale Development Agency and the University of Manchester. “Atom Valley could bring up to 20,000 skilled jobs to our part of Greater Manchester. For too long, growth has been concentrated in the south of the country and the centre of Manchester. “This is about making sure Rochdale is once again at the heart of Britain’s manufacturing future. Now we will be in pole position to contribute to the regional economy. articles.title: ‘Really nice’: an editor’s visit to the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Daily's editor visited the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with her little girl and found kind, efficient staff, a fully available menu and a welcome that earned a child's verdict: ‘really nice’.
articles.content_html:
There are plenty of ways to judge a new coffee shop. You can look at the menu, the speed of the service or whether it manages to make a quick stop feel pleasant. But after visiting the new Starbucks on Whitworth Road with my little girl, I found that the most telling review came from her.

“Really nice,” she said of the people working there. Two words, and a rather lovely assessment.

As the editor of Rochdale Daily, I spend a great deal of time looking at what opens, closes and changes across the borough. This time, rather than reporting on a launch, I wanted to experience the place as an ordinary customer — and a parent.

What stood out was the staff. They were kind, welcoming and efficient, handling our visit with the sort of ease that makes all the difference when you have a child alongside you. Good service does not need to be theatrical. Often, it is simply being treated warmly while everything runs as it should.

The full menu was available during our visit, too. There were no disappointing discoveries that something we wanted could not be ordered. It is a simple thing, but it matters: choice is only useful when the items are actually available.

The branch, which opened in August near Rochdale Infirmary and Dunelm, provides both indoor seating and a drive-through. For people visiting the hospital, passing along Whitworth Road or simply looking for a coffee stop, those options are convenient. But convenience alone is not what makes a customer want to return.

Children have an uncomplicated way of measuring an experience. They remember whether somebody was kind. They notice when they are made to feel welcome. My little girl did not care about the branding or the opening ceremony; she cared that the people were, in her words, “really nice”.

This was one family visit, not a claim that every visit will be identical. But the team deserve credit for getting the fundamentals right: kindness, efficiency and a menu we could actually order from.

Sometimes a new business makes its best first impression not through a grand announcement but through the people behind the counter. On our visit to Whitworth Road, Starbucks did exactly that.

Editor’s note: This is a first-hand editorial account of a visit, not a paid advertisement. For the original opening report, see Rochdale Daily’s article, “New Starbucks Drive-Through Opens on Whitworth Road”.

articles.title: Egerton Street, roadworks in Heywood from 20 October 2026
articles.excerpt: Rochdale Borough Council lists work affecting Egerton Street in Heywood; expected timings: 12midnight on Tuesday, 20 October 2026–11.59pm on Sunday, 1 November 2026.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale Borough Council has published a traffic notice for Egerton Street in Heywood. The council lists the expected start and finish as 12midnight on Tuesday, 20 October 2026–11.59pm on Sunday, 1 November 2026.

The council gives the reason as To install a new joint bay. The notice describes the affected area as follows: Part of Egerton Street will be temporarily closed. The closure will begin at the junction with Hind Hill Street and end 165 metres along the road in a westerly direction. No waiting will be allowed at any time in the closed section.

The published alternative route is Hind Hill Street, Market Place, York Street, Bamford Road, Market Street, Dawson Street, Bridge Street, Pilsworth Road and Egerton Street. These are the details in the council's current published record, rather than confirmation that work has started or finished. Readers travelling through the area can check the original Rochdale Borough Council notice for any subsequent amendments.

articles.title: Festival of Remembrance to bring borough together at Rochdale Town Hall on October 16
articles.excerpt: Rochdale will come together at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 16 October for a Festival of Remembrance honouring members of the Armed Forces community.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale will come together at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 16 October for a Festival of Remembrance honouring members of the Armed Forces community.

The event will feature music performed by military bands, an act of remembrance and historic war stories, alongside an opportunity for people to come together to reflect and reminisce.

The Festival of Remembrance is open to everyone and begins at 7pm.

Tickets are priced at £15 and include a pie and pea supper.

### Tickets and event information

Tickets are available through Rochdale Borough Council's event listing.

The council's listing gives the event date as Friday 16 October, with the programme beginning at 7pm at Rochdale Town Hall.

Rochdale Daily will continue to update this report if further information about the Festival of Remembrance is confirmed ahead of the event.
